subject: literature
title: KS3 Literature - Animal Farm Chapter 1: Reading Pack
description: Reading passages for Chapter 1 of Animal Farm, focused on Major's vision, equality, characterisation, and political context.

data.sourcePassage: Chapter 1 begins at Manor Farm after Mr Jones has been drinking. Once he has gone to bed, the animals gather in the barn because Old Major has called a meeting. This setting matters because it brings the whole farm together in one place and creates the feeling that something important is beginning. The scene also shows that the animals must meet in secret, which hints that human power depends on control and fear. Before any rebellion happens, Orwell presents the barn as a place where new ideas can be shared.

questions.question: Why do the animals gather in the barn?
questions.modelAnswer: They gather to hear Old Major speak.

questions.question: What does the secret meeting suggest about life under Mr Jones?
questions.modelAnswer: It suggests that the animals are not free and must hide their ideas because humans hold power over them.

questions.question: Why is the barn an important setting at the start of the novel?
questions.modelAnswer: The barn is important because it unites the animals and becomes the place where revolutionary ideas first take shape.

data.sourcePassage: Old Major tells the animals that the root of their suffering is man. He argues that humans consume without producing enough, while animals work hard and still go hungry. From this complaint, Major builds a vision of equality. He imagines a future in which animals keep the products of their own labour and no creature dominates another. His language is simple and direct, which makes the speech sound powerful. At the same time, Orwell lets readers notice how perfect the dream seems, planting the idea that such a vision may be hard to protect in reality.

questions.question: Who does Major blame for the animals' suffering?
How does Major link labour to equality?
questions.modelAnswer: He argues that animals should enjoy the results of their own work instead of being exploited by humans.

questions.question: Why might Orwell want Major's dream to sound almost too perfect?
questions.modelAnswer: Orwell may want readers to question whether ideal equality can survive once power is involved.

data.sourcePassage: Orwell carefully introduces Boxer and Clover so that readers respond warmly to them. Boxer is large and physically strong, but he is also gentle. Clover is motherly and alert to the needs of smaller animals. These details make both characters seem trustworthy rather than threatening. The source material points out that Orwell establishes this sympathy before the plot becomes more political. By doing that, he makes readers care about ordinary animals who will later suffer when the ideals of the revolution are betrayed.

questions.question: What quality of Boxer is mentioned alongside his strength?
Why does Orwell make Boxer and Clover seem trustworthy early on?
questions.modelAnswer: He wants readers to care about them so the later betrayal of the revolution feels more painful and important.

questions.question: What does Clover's behaviour reveal about her character?
questions.modelAnswer: It reveals that she is caring, protective, and concerned for weaker animals.

data.sourcePassage: The source pages connect Major's speech to the ideas of Karl Marx. Marx argued that workers were exploited by capitalists and that they might one day revolt. Orwell borrows parts of this argument when Major describes animals producing wealth while humans take the benefits. However, Orwell is not simply praising revolution. The chapter also prepares readers for a warning: even a movement that begins with equality can go wrong. That is why the later rise of the pigs becomes ironic. Chapter 1 matters because it introduces both the hope of change and the danger of future corruption.

questions.question: Which thinker is linked to Major's ideas in the source material?
questions.modelAnswer: The source links Major's ideas to Karl Marx.

questions.question: How does Orwell both use and question revolutionary ideas in Chapter 1?
questions.modelAnswer: He uses revolutionary language to show the appeal of equality, but he also hints that power can corrupt those ideals later.

questions.question: Why is the later behaviour of the pigs ironic when compared with Major's speech?
questions.modelAnswer: It is ironic because the pigs eventually act like the human oppressors that Major told the animals to reject.
